statement: Four bags P, Q, R and S all have different masses. They are compared on a two-pan balance three times. P and Q together balance R and S. P and S together are heavier than Q and R. P and R together are lighter than Q and S. Which bag is the heaviest?

choices.misconception: I saw P on the heavier pan in the second weighing and decided it must be the heaviest bag.
I saw Q on the heavier pan in the third weighing and decided it must be the heaviest bag.
I worked out the order of the bags correctly but read it the wrong way round, and picked the lightest bag.
I found that P and Q cannot be compared, and concluded that the heaviest bag cannot be found either.

hints: Write each weighing as an equation or an inequality using the letters for the masses.
Combine two weighings at a time. Adding or subtracting the balanced weighing to one of the uneven ones cancels two of the bags and compares the other two directly.
From P + Q = R + S and P + S > Q + R you get P > R and S > Q. Now do the same with the third weighing.

solutions.reliable: Use the letters for the masses. The weighings say P + Q = R + S, P + S > Q + R and Q + S > P + R. Adding the first two gives 2P + Q + S > Q + 2R + S, so P > R. Subtracting the first from the second gives S - Q > Q - S, so S > Q. Adding the first and third gives 2Q + P + S > P + 2R + S, so Q > R. Subtracting the first from the third gives S - P > P - S, so S > P. So S is heavier than P and Q, and both of those are heavier than R. S is the heaviest bag and R the lightest. For example, masses P = 2, Q = 3, R = 1 and S = 4 fit all three weighings. The transferable idea: combine balance results like equations, adding and subtracting them to cancel bags and compare the rest.
solutions.elegant: Think of starting from the balanced pans P + Q and R + S. Swapping Q and S between the pans makes the side holding S heavier, so S is heavier than Q. Swapping P and S also makes the side holding S heavier, so S is heavier than P. And S is heavier than R, since P + Q = R + S with S heavier than both P and Q forces R to be the lightest.

whyOnTest: Balance puzzles reward treating each weighing as an equation, and the traps are judging a bag by which pan it sat on rather than by combining the weighings.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
